This note explains the GitHub Actions workflows that check whether EJAM can be
installed. These workflows are intentionally separate from `R CMD check` because
they answer different questions.

## Quick install check

Workflow file: `.github/workflows/install-quick-check.yaml`

This is the low-cost install check. It runs on Ubuntu with the current release
of R. It installs only hard package dependencies first, then installs EJAM.

Automatic triggers:

- push to `development`
- pull request to `main`

Manual trigger:

- `workflow_dispatch`, with `install_source` set to either `local` or
  `github-sha`

Use the manual trigger when a branch changes package dependencies, installation
code, or workflow files and you want a quick install check without running the
full release matrix.

What it proves:

- `local`: the checked-out source tree installs.
- `github-sha`: the same commit can be installed from GitHub by commit SHA.

## Release and user install checks

Workflow file: `.github/workflows/install-release-user-check.yaml`

This workflow is deliberately more expensive. It is for release validation and
for testing installation paths that users are likely to use.

Automatic triggers:

- push of a tag matching `v*`
- GitHub Release published

Manual trigger:

- `workflow_dispatch`, with a `ref` such as `development`, `v4.2024.0`, or a commit SHA
- optional `expected_version`, matching `Version` in that ref's `DESCRIPTION`
- `test_scope` set to one of:

| `test_scope` | What runs | Jobs |
|---|---|---|
| `user-style` (default) | the clean-machine `pak` install only | 2 |
| `full-matrix` | the prepared-runner matrix only | 18 |
| `both` | the prepared-runner matrix and the clean-machine `pak` install | 20 |
| `ubuntu-only` | the Ubuntu rows of the prepared-runner matrix only | 6 |

`ubuntu-only` is the cheapest way to check that a branch, tag, or SHA installs
and loads. It skips Windows and macOS.

The two kinds of job answer different questions. Both end by loading EJAM with
`library(EJAM)` and checking its version, so neither tests EJAM's code beyond
loading it.

### Prepared-runner matrix (`full-matrix`)

This job tests Linux, Windows, and macOS, with `oldrel-1` and `release` R, and
three install methods, for 18 combinations:

- `local`: install the checked-out source tree with `utils::install.packages()`
  and `INSTALL_opts`
- `github-ref`: install from GitHub by branch, tag, or SHA using
  `remotes::install_github()`
- `url-tarball`: install the GitHub source tarball using `remotes::install_url()`

Before installing EJAM, each job prepares the runner the way a developer's
machine would be prepared:

- On Ubuntu, it installs system libraries with `apt-get` (GDAL, GEOS, PROJ,
  udunits, cairo, and others).
- On macOS, it installs system libraries with Homebrew (GDAL, cairo, udunits,
  freetype, and others).
- On every runner, it installs EJAM's hard R package dependencies from
  DESCRIPTION, using `r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies`.

EJAM itself is then installed with `install.packages()` or `remotes`, not
`pak`. The workflow uses `remotes` for `github-ref` and `url-tarball` because
those checks need
`INSTALL_opts = c("--with-keep.source", "--install-tests", "--no-test-load")`.
`pak::pkg_install()` is preferred for ordinary user installs, but it does not
accept those `R CMD INSTALL` options.

A pass here shows that EJAM's source installs and loads on each platform, given
its dependencies. It does not show that a new user can get those dependencies.

### Clean-machine `pak` install (`user-style`)

This job tests Windows and macOS with the current release of R. It skips every
preparation step above: no Homebrew libraries, no `apt-get`, and no
`setup-r-dependencies`. It starts from a plain R installation and follows the
[installation instructions](installing.html):

```r
options(timeout = 600)
install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("Public-Environmental-Data-Partners/EJAM@REF",
                 dependencies = NA, upgrade = FALSE)
library(EJAM)
```

`dependencies = NA` installs the hard dependencies (Depends, Imports,
LinkingTo), not Suggests, which matches the installation instructions.

For a manual run, `REF` is the `ref` workflow input. For a GitHub Release
published event, `REF` is that release's tag, for example `v4.2024.0`.

This job catches problems the prepared-runner matrix cannot see, because those
problems happen while dependencies are installed:

- `pak` handles dependency resolution differently from `remotes`, including the
  GitHub-only packages in DESCRIPTION's `Remotes:` field.
- On macOS, every dependency must install without Homebrew libraries. That
  works when CRAN has ready-built (binary) packages for the current R. A dependency that must be compiled from source, for
  example right after a new R release, fails here but passes in the
  prepared-runner matrix.

If the prepared-runner matrix passes and this job fails, look first at
dependencies and `pak`, not at EJAM's own code.

### What each trigger proves

- tag pushes prove that a specific tag can be installed by local source,
  GitHub ref, and GitHub source tarball.
- release published events prove that the latest GitHub Release can be installed
  with the public `pak`-based instructions on Windows and macOS.
- manual runs can test a branch, tag, or SHA before deciding whether to create
  or publish a release.

## Branches and workflow file versions

GitHub Actions uses the workflow file from the branch or ref that triggers the
event, with some event-specific details. In practice, keep workflow files as
similar as possible in `development`, `main`, and the active preparation branch unless
there is a deliberate reason for a branch-specific workflow.

Manual `workflow_dispatch` runs are easiest to use once the workflow file exists
on the repository's default branch. The Actions page can then run the workflow
against a selected branch, tag, or SHA, depending on the workflow inputs.

Recommended workflow promotion:

- Edit and test workflow changes on the active working branch first.
- Integrate vX workflow changes into `vX.20YY.0-prep` first. Keep `development`
  on the current version line until team authorizes the version change/transition.
- At that transition, bring the approved changes into `development`, then
  `main` through the release process before relying on them for release validation.
- For historical install checks, select an existing release tag rather than
  maintaining a separate branch per data vintage.

The branch workflow proves only that its branch or commit installs as the version
in `DESCRIPTION`. It does not prove that a release tag installs until that tag
exists and its tag-triggered workflow passes. In particular, the preparation
branch name does not activate v4 data or change its package version.
